subtopic: CULTURAL AND INFORMATION AGREEMENTS WITH NATO COUNTRIES
CULTURAL AND INFORMATION AGREEMENTS WITH NATO COUNTRIES
speechtext:
1.	With which NATO member countries has Canada reached bilateral cultural and information agreements and which fields do these agreements cover?
2.	Where there are no such agreements or limited agreements only, what is Canada's policy in the following fields (a) exchanges of cultural programs (theatres, films, television exhibitions) (b) exchanges of students-number planned-exchange procedure (c) exchanges of teachers and research workers-number planned-exchange procedure (fellowship) (d) equivalence of diplomas-system used and future plans (e) exchange of young workers-numbers-procedure used (f) exchanges through leisure activities-holiday camps-travel?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CULTURAL AND INFORMATION AGREEMENTS WITH NATO COUNTRIES
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of External Affairs is concerned: 1. The only country with which Canada has signed a general cultural agreement is France. This agreement which was signed on November 17, 1965, covers the fields of academic, scientific, technical and cultural exchanges. In 1963 Canada and France signed an agreement on the co-production of films.
The government's policy, now that a general cultural agreement has been signed with
France, is to develop cultural programs and explore the possibilities of entering into similar cultural agreements with a number of other countries, many of which are members of NATO, particularly those from which substantial groups in the population of Canada have come. However, because of the cultural heritage English speaking Canada shares with Britain and the U.S.A., our cultural relations with these countries are characterized by informality and it has not been felt necessary to have them formalized through agreements.
2.	Where no agreement exists, the initiative is left entirely to public and private organizations of a cultural or educational character such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the National Film Board, the Canada Council, the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, etc.

subtopic: CANADIAN CULTURAL ACTIVITIES UNDER NATO
CANADIAN CULTURAL ACTIVITIES UNDER NATO
speechtext: What part Is being played by Canada in the cultural field, with regard to member countries of NATO, by private cultural associations (a) of a general nature (b) of a more specifically Atlantic nature?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN CULTURAL ACTIVITIES UNDER NATO
speechtext:
Numerous Canadians of European origin, many of whom have come from countries which are members of NATO, seek to maintain cultural links with their European home country. There are consequently an enormous number of private cultural associations in Canada which have as their main purpose the pursuit of cultural relations and exchanges with countries of Europe including NATO countries. In addition there are Canadian associations with a wide range of interests and activities which have international connections. Because of the similarities of Canadian background and traditions with the countries of western Europe and the United States, by far the greater part of the international connections of these associations are with the countries of the Atlantic area.
The activities of the very large number of associations involved are their own concern. Since they are not subject to governmental supervision, reports on their activities are not made to the government.

subtopic: MOTOR CAR PRICE DIFFERENTIAL BETWEEN CANADA AND U.S.
MOTOR CAR PRICE DIFFERENTIAL BETWEEN CANADA AND U.S.
speechtext:
1.	Has the government taken or is it taking any act to remove the price differential, reported to be as much as $3,000 on the more expensive models, between similar cars sold in the U.S.A. and in Canada and, if so, what action?
2.	Are cars manufactured in Canada sold at a lower price in the U.S.A. than they are in Canada
January 23, 1967

and, If so (a) for what reason (b) who benefits from the extra cost of the ones sold in Canada?
3.	Are cars manufactured in the U.S.A. sold at a lower price in the U.S.A. than they are in Canada and, if so (a) for what reason (b) who benefits from the extra cost of the ones sold in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: MOTOR CAR PRICE DIFFERENTIAL BETWEEN CANADA AND U.S.
speechtext:
1.	Traditionally there has been a sizeable price differential between similar cars sold in the United States and in Canada. This situation arose because of the fact that the market for motor vehicles is much larger in the United States than in Canada. Consequently, vehicle manufacturers in the United States were able to realize the economies of large scale production and specialization. On the other hand, because of the limited size of the Canadian market, it was not possible to specialize and costs and prices reflected the disadvantages of shorter production runs in Canada.
The government has taken positive steps to substantially reduce the differential in prices between Canada and the United States. One of the central features of the Canada-United States automotive agreement has been the elimination of the tariff barriers which prevented Canadian companies from gaining access to wider markets. Consequently, Canadian companies are now able to rationalize production and achieve significant increases in growth and efficiency. Although differentials in prices still exist, progress achieved under the automotive program has already resulted in a very significant reduction of these differentials.
In 1965, prices of volume models of motor vehicles made in Canada were reduced and the average level of the price differential was diminished from 8 per cent to less than 5 per cent. In 1966, the differentials were again reduced. As the economies of volume production are more fully realized, it is anticipated that the forces of competition will bring about a further diminution of the remaining price differentials.
2.	If the Canadian companies wish to export their vehicles to the United States, they must sell at a competitive price in that market, otherwise they would have to forego the extensive exports which have been made possible by the automotive program. The loss of these exports would, in turn, reverse the rationalization which has taken place in Canada and could result in an increase in costs and prices in this country. The terms and conditions of sales of Canadian made vehicles in other countries are, of course, private commercial transactions between sellers and buyers. Prices in these markets, which may vary
Questions
considerably depending on local market conditions, are determined by competitive forces in the particular area.
Although costs and prices have been substantially reduced in Canada, it has not yet been possible to realize the full cost benefits of increased production and rationalization. It is doubtful that anyone benefits from the remaining higher costs of production in Canada.
3.	International price comparisons, to be meaningful and valid, have to be based on an examination of actual sales under identical or very similar conditions. In the case of automobiles sold in Canada and the United States it is exceedingly difficult to find such closely comparable actual transactions. There are a number of factors which influence and determine the levels of prices and which have differential effects in the two countries. One of the most obvious is the rate of exchange between the currencies of the two countries. Other factors include variations in transportation costs between the factory and the retailers, the levels of sales tax, which vary from state to state and province to province, dealer margins differ from agency to agency and the range of options normally differs from car to car. Even a single dealer's price for the same model may differ according to the circumstances of a specific sale. It is possible to say, however, that prices of practically all motor vehicles sold in Canada, whether of domestic manufacture or imported, are now much closer to the price levels prevailing in the United States.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RATIFICATION OF INTERNATIONAL COVENANTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON RATIFICATION OF INTERNATIONAL COVENANTS
speechtext:
May I take this opportunity to reply to a question asked by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition on Friday last regarding the ratification of the international covenants on human rights. The three covenants which 23033-765J
Inquiries of the Ministry were adopted at the last session of the general assembly were (1) an international covenant on economic, social and cultural rights; (2) an international covenant on civil and political rights; and (3) an optional protocol to the latter covenant concerning the right of petition by individuals for the redress of alleged violations of the rights described in the civil and political covenant.
Basically these covenants are designed to give effect, by means of the binding obligations of international treaties, to the principles embodied in the universal declaration of human rights which was adopted by the general assembly in 1948. They represent a major piece of work by the United Nations and have been under consideration for 14 years.
Their adoption last year by the assembly represented, I believe, a significant step forward by the international community in the field of human rights. Canada voted for the adoption of all three instruments, and over the years during which they have been under consideration we have been privileged to make some constructive contributions to the drafting of those instruments.
A substantial number of the provisions of the covenants fall within provincial jurisdiction, so we are consulting the governments of the provinces in order to obtain their views. This is, I think, an essential step with regard to the implementation of these provisions. In addition we have set up an interdepartmental committee to review the covenants as finally approved last December from the federal point of view to the end of ensuring signature and ratification by Canada at the earliest possible date. However, before the covenants can be submitted to the House of Commons I believe we should consult with the provinces with respect to those provisions which concern the provinces from the standpoint of implementation, and await the report of the interdepartmental committee.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON RATIFICATION OF INTERNATIONAL COVENANTS
speechtext:
If I may be allowed to say so, in view of the lengthy statement made by the Prime Minister, I agree with him that these agreements are of far reaching significance and that they represent a distinct step forward in the preservation of fundamental freedoms in all parts of the world.
However, in view of the important decision I think in 1936, when the Privy Council decided that while these undertakings have treaty obligations they do not in any way cause a
January 23, 1967

Inquiries of the Ministry signatory nation, such as Canada, to be bound in respect of those things that are within provincial jurisdiction, I ask the Prime Minister whether, in view of the great importance of the two treaty arrangements and the third protocol arrangement, he would convene a dominion-provincial conference on this question so the provinces, realizing the importance of these treaty obligations, would be prepared, in so far as the treaties themselves are concerned, to accept them as necessary and material to peace in the world?

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RATIFICATION OF INTERNATIONAL COVENANTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the right hon. gentleman's suggestion might be a very useful one indeed, but I suggest that before a conference is called we could perhaps deal with this matter at the next federal-provincial conference of heads of governments. The provinces then would have a chance to examine the conventions and give us their views in writing, with more consideration than at this time. We have taken that initial step, and I hope that before long we can take the step suggested by the right hon. gentleman.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RATIFICATION OF INTERNATIONAL COVENANTS

As a
supplementary question I would ask the Prime Minister whether he would discuss with the provincial governments, and also refer to the interdepartmental committee, the question of whether some of these basic freedoms to which he has referred might be appropriately incorporated into the fundamental law of Canada, which is the constitution of Canada.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON RATIFICATION OF INTERNATIONAL COVENANTS
speechtext: That is another question, Mr. Speaker, and it will have to be considered when we have reached the point when we are considering the present constitution, its amendment and revision. Undoubtedly one of the matters to be reviewed at that time will be the role of the federal government in the whole field of external affairs. I would not like to consider that matter in relation to these particular conventions at this time. I would hope it could wait until we get to the general subject of constitutional amendment and revision, and we hope that will not be too long.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, January 20, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-231, to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other acts in consequence thereof, and to enact other consequential provisions-Mr. Pickersgill-Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Order. Clauses 1, 16 as amended, 22 to 28 inclusive, 50, 58, 59 and 74, together with the schedule, have yet to be disposed of by the committee. When the committee rose on Friday last clause 58 was under discussion.
On clause 58.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we rose on Friday afternoon we had spent only 10 or 15 minutes on what, within the next two or three hours, will be a last ditch stand made on behalf of the ports of Halifax and Saint John. I am glad to see that the Minister of Finance is in the chamber, because it is money that we will be talking about.
First of all I should like to deal in depth with the amendment moved by the minister on Friday providing for protection or certain clauses that have been long standing on Canadian statutes, going back to 1903, 1911 and 1914. On behalf of those directly associated with the ports of Halifax and Saint John I want to tell the minister that his amendment is not adequate.
Earlier the minister chided me by saying that I spoke from ignorance on matters of transportation. I am prepared to accept that I do. I have never pretended to be an expert on transportation. Anything I say this afternoon will not be born of malice, and if it arises from ignorance I only hope the minister will be kind enough to overlook my very junior position. Despite the assurances the minister gave us two or three weeks ago that the amendment he would move would be adequate, now that we have read it we can see that it is not at all adequate.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I intend to propose a substitute amendment to that of the minister which will have to be dealt with at the proper time and place. The minister's amendment to clauses 58 and 59 states in part:
Nething in this act except section 334-
Transportation
We agree with that first part, but we are then hauled up short because of the exception in respect of section 334. Without going into detail let me be brutally honest with the minister by telling him that the reaction in Halifax has been expressed in the form of the question 'When do we quit?" The amendment continues:
-shall be construed to affect any obligation imposed upon any railway company subject to the jurisdiction of parliament by any other act or any agreement made pursuant thereto requiring the company
(a)	to maintain rates on export traffic-
There is no mention of import traffic. The amendment continues:
-moving through any Canadian seaport located in the "select territory"-
Again I suggest to the minister that the select territory provision does not go far enough so far as those who are most directly involved in Halifax are concerned. The amendment continues:
-as defined by sections 2, 7 and 12 of the Maritime Freight Rates Act at a specified level, or at a level specified in relation to other rates; or
(b)	to route export traffic through Canadian seaports.
The minister will have to explain the relationship between (a) and (b) before we will know whether they should be included in our proposed amendment.
There are four areas in which this amendment appears to fall seriously short of our intent. First it fails to mention import traffic but deals only with export traffic. We are not unmindful of the fact that perhaps Canadian dollars and cents are going to foreign countries in subsidization of traffic which-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would permit a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: The purpose of this amendment, as the hon. gentleman properly pointed out, is to maintain the law which now exists and to make sure that it is not touched in any way except in that one respect. I will have a word to say about that later. Does the hon. member know of any statute at all that applies to import traffic? I do not know of any statute that does so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
The minister is absolutely right. What I am saying is that some concern exists because it does not. Perhaps there is good reason for this not covering import traffic, but I simply ask why it does not, and I

January 23, 1967
Transportation
hope the minister will provide that answer in a few minutes.
There is an exception in section 334 in relation to export traffic. All it provides is that as long as the rates are compensatory, traffic going to United States ports will be the same as to Saint John and Halifax. That is based on the general position which existed when the statutes were placed on the books in the first 15 or 20 years of this century, or some 45 to 50 years ago. That general proposition may have been valid at that time but it is no longer valid today. The minister knows that in order for the rates to be economically feasible the C.N.R. will have to lower its rates, particularly if it is to adhere to the principle of the bill that is before us. We will refer to that situation at some length.
The third shortcoming of this amendment is its lack of reference to North Atlantic-United States ports. The closest it comes to any reference of that kind is in (b) which states:
(b) to route export traffic through Canadian seaports.
Perhaps that was the intent of the old act, but the most charitable thing that can be said about it is that it is not clear what areas are to be protected or how they are to be protected. As the minister agrees, all we are protecting are the old sections of the act. They are being put in proper context.
Perhaps it would be wise at this point to review them briefly. There are three, the first dating from 1903 and the second from 1911. They can be found in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the transport and communications committee, at page 2537 in volume No. 37.
These three sections appear in the brief presented by the maritimes transportation commission. The first refers to the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company in 1903, which provided that-
-the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination, shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports.
This was renewed in 1911 by section 13, chapter 6 which refers to the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company. This particular section provided that:
-the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports.
Again we find that chapter 20, acts of 1914, re the Canadian Northern Railway System provided that:

-the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall not be greater via Canadian ports than it would be via United States ports; ... and that the Canadian Northern and the several constituent and subsidiary companies shall not in any manner within its power or control directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of any such freight by routes other than those above provided.
These statutes were valid 50 years ago and, indeed, their concept is not only valid today but absolutely essential to the survival of the ports of Saint John and Halifax. We suggest that by just going that far the job which must be done will not be done.
We intend to deal with the fourth shortcoming of this amendment at some length this afternoon. It is, of course, the fact that there is a restriction as to "select ports" as defined in sections 2, 7 and 12 of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. As the minister well knows, the select area is simply that area which encompasses the two meaningful ports in the maritimes, Halifax and Saint John.
We have all observed the erosion and whittling away of the effects of t he Maritime Freight Rates Act on traffic into and out of those two ports. Halifax no longer enjoys parity with Saint John. It is about time we stopped this game in the maritimes, as someone put it not long ago, of an indigent taking from an indigent to form a greater needy area. What we are doing is taking away from each other, and there is nothing to protect us in this regard. The economy of our area and the ports of Halifax and Saint John depend almost entirely on transportation. The minister does not need to be told this. In no small way this is the basis of the principle upon which we will propose an amendment.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
We have heard the arguments about the effect on our secondary manufacturing industry of the national transportation system. We have been told over and over and over again for 150 years how absolutely necessary it has been and is to have an adequate transportation system. In the old days it used to be water; now it is our rail system. On the basis of our rail system, what secondary manufacturing industry we enjoy has survived and grown economically.
The whole basis of this bill seems to be cutting away from that principle. If we are to survive at all economically, if we are to foster and encourage the development of secondary industry, our national transportation system must continue to be a viable instrument of not only national but regional development. It
January 23, 1967



must not die; it must remain. As a matter of fact, it must be something very precious, close and dear to us, particularly during the next 10 or 15 years.
The underlying assumption, I suppose, to set the background in this respect, is that the interests of Canada as a whole demand that there remain in the maritime provinces a substantial number of people who are able and capable of putting their talents and brains to work in the development of secondary industry. If we lose sight of this principle and assumption, and indeed we seem to be heading toward that position now with this new piece of legislation, the federal authority will have to find something else to embrace and make use of to assist the economy of this area.
It has been said recently by meaningful and very responsible people in the maritime area that we have on the one hand the federal authority, through the Atlantic Development Board, pouring millions and millions of dollars into the development of the Atlantic economy, the study of methods of development, the encouragement through certain services of industrial parks and so on, the area incentive program under which God only knows how much money is being spent in the maritimes, and then we depart from that principle in respect of the one thing that is absolutely necessary-as a matter of fact, it is the only thing that is absolutely necessary-to the orderly and economic development of secondary manufacturing. I refer to rail transportation. We come along with this measure and cut the ground out from under that orderly and economic development.
It is not enough to stand here today and make these remarks without suggesting improvements in this area. We now understand that the special study has been completed and should be in the minister's hands very soon, much sooner than we anticipated. Perhaps the minister could shed more light on that subject. We thought this study would be handed down some time next month and placed before us. The study might clarify many of the doubts in our minds. However, I expect we will wait considerably longer before receiving it. I say again that it is not enough for us to accept what might be in eight, ten months' or a year's time a very profitable position for us to adopt. I believe these principles have to be built in and safeguarded in the bill itself. They should be built in in terms of positive and very clear statements.
Transportation
In case the minister has not bothered to look at the shipping tonnages recently, it is rather interesting to note the figures for Halifax, Saint John, Montreal, and Quebec. They show what has happened to foreign traffic coming into Canada in the last ten years. I will not go through all the statistics but just refer to seven or eight years. I take first the 1957-58 shipping season. I am taking the total of the eight winter months for those two years. I have included December because it is a part month, as is March, but essentially the months are January, February, March and December. In the 1957-58 season Halifax and Saint John enjoyed 1,627,000 tons of shipping. In that same four-month period covering December, January, February and March, Montreal and Quebec enjoyed 309,000 tons, every last ounce of which was handled in the first ten days of December and the last ten days of March.
I should now like to quote the figures for the 1961, 1963 and 1964 shipping seasons, the same eight months. They are for general tonnage and do not include petroleum, wheat or anything like that. They refer to general cargo, which is the only type of cargo meaningful to our economy, in terms of dollar impact. The ports of Halifax and Saint John handled 1,-
437,000	tons of cargo. That figure is down
200.000	tons. What do we see in regard to Montreal and Quebec? We see a rise from
309.000	tons to over 518,000 tons. In 1965-66, taking those eight months, Halifax and Saint John dropped off to 1,377,000 tons while Montreal and Quebec went up to 648,000 tons. The minister knows the 1966 figures. I think there has been more traffic in and out of the port of Montreal in the last six weeks than has been in and out of both the ports of Halifax and Saint John in the last two years. There is no work on our waterfront.
But look at the position of Montreal and Quebec. Go back 100 years. At that time there was no traffic in and out of the ports of Montreal and Quebec, absolutely none. But in 1966, in the period I have quoted, 233 foreign-going ships cleared the port of Montreal. And these figures are already two weeks old. How many have been in and out since then? I cite these figures because they show so dramatically what has happened. Traffic is not coming to the port of Halifax; it is going to the ports of Montreal and Quebec.
There is good reason for this and it is an understandable one. Perhaps because of my very junior and ignorant position in the house I have never been in a position where I could

January 23, 1967
Transportation
criticize the minister or the government about winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river. However, I do not believe criticism is necessarily the proper attitude. Indeed, I could go much further and ask the minister to give us a few dollars so that we may convert the port of Halifax to deep water shipping. There is need right now for positive planning in this regard. It has been done in connection with the Delaware estuary running into Maryland, where it was found that for a piddling $200 million ships could be moved into that area. The government does not necessarily have to assign an icebreaker to the port of Halifax. If they wanted to they could put a crew in there with picks and shovels to keep the slush out. They could make it a free port up to the lakehead if they wished. But we should get something in return, and quickly. I do not want to go into these other points in any detail, but I draw these matters to the attention of the minister for his consideration.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The amendment I have before me is not typed but I have many amendments in front of me which I propose to move one at a time. I will start with the least line of resistance. A little later I will move an amendment along these general lines. It reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything contained in this or any other act, rail rates (to and from shipside) on export and import traffic to or from eastern ports, as defined in section 329A of this act, from or to the points of origin or destination shall at no time be greater via any such Canadian port than via any other such Canadian port or via United States north Atlantic ports.
We do not intend to move this amendment lightly. The minister grins. I should like to ask him whether in commenting on the amendment he could suggest what else can be done in order to save the ports of Halifax and Saint John. Unless the government expends money to re-equip these ports, and particularly to equip the port of Halifax for the advent of the deep-water mammoth ships about which people, are talking these days, unless the minister has something he can suggest and is prepared to do immediately, then some action in the nature of the amendment which I read will have to be seriously considered.
No less an authority than Mr. Mingo, who for a long time has been chairman of the port of Halifax commission and who does not pretend to be an expert on rail rates, port parity or port structures-and since he does not share my particular political pursuasion I can quote him as being an objective authority-has said that unless something is

done now the end is in sight for the ports of Halifax and Saint John. The minister was good enough to stand this section, and we took his amendment home to Halifax to let the people there see it because they are the ones who are concerned. The opinion which was voiced there was that the amendment did not do anything. If that is all we are going to get we might as well give up. Indeed, I think the minister probably heard Mr. Mingo's opinion when he was in Halifax on the annual ports day.
Mr. Mingo in his address to that august gathering of shipping people from Halifax and Saint John suggested that indeed it is perhaps time that the minister and the government gave consideration to the establishment of a board, either within the present context of the new transportation commission or outside it. He did not elaborate on the suggestion but he made it quite plain that unless a board composed of people living in the area who have dealt with rail and water transportation over the years is established, all we will be doing is treading water. I suggest that treading water in any field is tantamount to becoming stagnant and in fact going backwards. The minister is very much aware of these points.
The other things that come immediately to mind are so obvious that they do not need repeating at this time so I will not go into them in any depth. The minister is aware of the fact that the unemployment situation in the maritimes is very serious at present. The figures which were published on January 15 showed that the national average is 4.5 or 4.6 per cent while the figure for the maritimes is 10.7 per cent. One does not have to spell out the effects resulting from the loss of winter traffic, the loss to longshoremen, ship brokers and stevedoring companies and the loss to the port of Halifax in fees and costs. One does not have to point out the urgency of correcting this situation before it hits rock bottom. I suggest that we are close to rock bottom and the only way to avoid reaching it is to move meaningfully in the direction of an adequate port parity structure which would involve not only the ports of Halifax and Saint John but also the United States north Atlantic ports and all the ports up to and including Montreal.
We realize that this will cost the government a lot of money and we are not making suggestions without being aware of the effects they might have. Somehow or other we have to create an atmosphere in which we can keep people in the maritimes, in which we can keep their intelligence and their brains at home. We
January 23, 1967

must keep our labour pools fluid and accessible to new industry which might want to come in. The only way in which we can do so is through transportation. It surprises me, now that we are discussing port parity, to see so few people here from the maritimes. Perhaps they are not interested. Perhaps the minister has made sure that they are not too far away and possibly during the course of the afternoon they may come in and contribute in a small way toward making the minister a little more pliant than he appears to be. We would welcome any comments he might have.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I should like to support the hon. member for Halifax. I have a few thoughts I want to put on the record which will bring the matter up to date so far as I am concerned. Over a period of time from about the turn of the century a port parity structure was built up by which the eastern ports were guaranteed that export and import rates would be maintained at parity with rates to United States ports. Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this amendment, as I explained originally is to ensure that every statutory protection that exists in the law of Canada at the present time to provide for specific rates, parity in rates or the routing of traffic through the ports of Halifax and Saint John shall remain in force notwithstanding anything in this bill.
The hon. member for Halifax properly said earlier this afternoon that some of these rates which might at one time have been compensatory might conceivably be argued to be not compensatory now and we might therefore be eroding this protection. Hon. members can tell that I thought the same way the hon. member thought because I anticipated his objection and had this mimeographed copy of the amendment ready. I confess that I woke in the middle of the night, the night after I moved this amendment, and began thinking about it. I thought what I really should have said is, "notwithstanding section 334" instead of having made the exception. When I talked

about this with the law officer advising me he said, "You know, there is a much simpler way to do it and that is to strike the words out". In any event it seems to me that there can be no doubt whatever that everything that is now in the law protecting those ports will remain in the law. This amendment will remove any possible doubt.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert asked whether I had asked the law officers of my department to check the law, to ascertain what the various laws having to do with the matter were. I think it would have been much better if we had been able to spell all of them out. The hon. member also rightly said that some of these laws have been interpreted by the courts. It is very easy, if you try to specify these things and you do not know for sure what all of them are, to leave something out. A compilation is being made. All the law is being thoroughly searched at the present time, and this search has been going on for several months. It involves searching a great proportion of all the statutes of Canada enacted since confederation and many legal decisions.
To be absolutely sure that nothing is left out, if we say that everything that is part of the law of Canada remains the law of Canada there can be no danger of any kind of mistake. As soon as this compilation has been completed I intend to make it available to hon. members and other interested parties for their information and to bring it to the attention of the new commission as soon as possible so that it may have an opportunity to peruse it.
I do not think hon. members will expect me to say anything more about winter navigation on the St. Lawrence than has been said already. It is a subject on which there are continuing differences of view. I can only commend the very reasonable and sensible attitude taken by the hon. members for Halifax and Saint John-Albert. They do not believe, if navigation during winter becomes technically feasible, that it can be stopped by law. They do not expect it to be, and I am sure all reasonable people take this view. That does not mean, of course, that we should not do everything possible to maximize traffic through the ports of Saint John and Halifax and other eastern ports where we can maximize traffic.
Though this is strictly not relevant to the clause, I wish to reiterate the position I have taken. Since I have been Minister of Transport the National Harbours Board has been

given tangible evidence of my disposition, because I am the minister who has to take responsibility for its budget. My position has been that in every instance where we have had any sound reason to believe that improvements either to the port of Halifax or the port of Saint John would result in increased traffic or would attract more traffic-and sometimes it was a bit of a gamble-we have been willing to go ahead with those improvements, and considerable improvements have been made and are being made in both ports. Some of the most notable improvements in both ports have been to the grain handling facilities and to the facilities for handling general cargo.
I assure the hon. member for Halifax that as long as 1 am Minister of Transport-and I believe this will be the attitude of any government-if there is any reasonable prospect, and I believe there is, that the new superships will come into service and if, with the proper facilities, they can use the port of Halifax which perhaps is the only port on the east coast with sufficient depth of water and other conditions to make it possible for these ships to be used, the facilities will be put there. They can be built faster than the ships. I do not think we can have any doubts that these developments will take place as rapidly as possible.
With respect to the point raised by the hon. gentleman about imports, quite frankly I know of no statute that now protects anything having to do with import traffic. I know of no statutory requirement-and it is rather difficult to see how one would do what the hon. member has suggested-which gives statutory protection to import traffic. I would hesitate to import the word "import" into the law, if I might make an inexcusable pun, without considering carefully what its real effect might be.

Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has said, and I appreciate the spirit in which he said it, I will have to make fairly extensive observations on this clause. It is the clause that provides basically for the transitional subsidies to the railways. It provides that these transitional subsidies shall be reduced year by year by a certain fraction until they ultimately disappear. There is provision also for certain specific payments that would be made to the railways in respect of certain services that may be imposed upon them in the national interest. These payments would replace some part of these subsidies at a time when the subsidies were sufficiently reduced so that the railways would require the other money to make up the difference.

In other words, the railways will not get both the transitional subsidies and the specific payments for specific services. When the total of the specific payments equals the transitional subsidies, the transitional subsidies would not be paid any longer-at least, the amount would not be paid twice. The other day the committee saw fit to disregard my entreaties and knocked out of clause 50 the proposed new section 329 of the Railway Act. I believe, sir, that in so doing what the committee was seeking to assert was that they did not feel parliament should direct the new commission to conduct a mandatory review of the revenues and costs connected with grain rates. Although I did not like the decision of the committee, I respect it. If my interpretation of the decision made by the committee is a correct one, I am not going to suggest that this basic decision be reversed. In other words, I am not going to ask hon. members to insist upon a mandatory review by the commission of the financial effects of the carriage of grain as prescribed in this bill.
However, the adoption of the amendment had some perhaps not incidental but ancillary effects that are quite important. It had the effect, for example, of removing the protection for freight rates on a great many grain products other than wheat and flour, which I am sure most hon. members who voted for that amendment had no intention or desire of removing. It is quite true the hon. member for York South made a statement that in clause 15 of the bill there was adequate power of review of any matter that the government might wish to have reviewed. I feel I would prefer not to rely upon clause 15, particularly when the committee has expressed the view that it does not want a mandatory review of these matters.
The hon. member for Acadia, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and others pointed out, and I thought there was some substance to their argument, that by asking parliament to require the commission to make this review a presumption was being created that the rates on grain were not compensatory. I have no desire to ask a committee or the house to create any such presumption. Indeed, in this matter I was seeking to be completely neutral and to leave it to the commission to determine what the facts were. I do agree that in perhaps a sentimental or a notional way it might be said, if you demand a mandatory review of something, you imply a certain conclusion even before the review is made. I believe we should not do anything that would 
leave any such implication because I know how strongly people feel about this in western Canada.
I do not want to do anything that is going to look to anybody as though there is any bias in this matter because I assure hon. members there is not. I do believe that one or two members-I have not reviewed the debates sufficiently to recall who they were-felt it would always be open to the railway to ask for such a review. Then the onus of asking for it, the onus of proving the case, would be entirely on the railways. I accept that as a reasonable proposition. It occurred to me, therefore, that one way in which we could accomplish all the incidental things that I feel need to be accomplished in this bill without asking the committee to reverse itself on the main point that there should not be a mandatory review imposed upon the commission, would be by an amendment I am going to suggest. There are one or two minor technical points, but so far as the main point is concerned the amendment would provide that in the case of any statutory rate, not merely grain rates but any statutory rate, provided in this bill, the railways, not earlier than two years after the coming into force of the bill, could apply to have any statutory rate reviewed by the commission. The rates we have just dealt with in the new clause 59 would come within this category too.
The fact that the rate would be reviewed could not mean a change in the rate. This would be a review of revenues and costs. Then there would be a recommendation to the governor in council on whether any relief should be afforded to the railways. The way this would work would be that the railways would have to ask for the review. They would have to take the onus and provide the proof. They would have to make their case, and if they made their case there would be no obligation on the government to provide the relief. The government would be told what relief, in the opinion of the commission, would be desirable. Then the government would have to exercise its discretion whether to bring something before parliament.
It seems to me that this procedure would meet all the objections that were voiced to the other procedure. This procedure applies to all statutory rates, and it would apply also to all rates that are set by the commission. If under clause 16 the commission sets aside a rate and substitutes its own judgment, then two years and not less than two years after such substituted rate was set a railway could claim it

We have made fairly adequate provision for appeals by shippers against the unfairness of rates. We have said that one of the principles of this bill is that if statutory and regulatory obligations are placed upon the railways they are entitled to be compensated for those things out of the treasury. Here we have something that does not appear to me to be open to any of the objections to which section 329 may have been open, though personally I did not think it was objectionable. However, the committee chose to think it was. But here at any rate no one can say that there is any presumption. The government does not have to take any initiative, nor does the commission; it is the railways themselves that have to make the application. Therefore there is no presumption placed in the bill, any more than there is a presumption in giving a shipper the right under clause 16 to say that the railways are taking an undue advantage of him in one case as opposed to another.
In the same amendment in a new section 471 I also propose to replace the definition of grain rates, which I believe was inadvertently thrown out like the baby with the bath water. I do not think any hon. member in any part of this chamber would want this situation to persist.
I am also going to make another suggestion. A very eloquent and persuasive plea was made by my hon. friend from Vancouver Quadra, which found an echo on the other side of the house, if I may so describe the venerable member for Kootenay West, in connection with rates on grain into British Columbia for domestic purposes. I feel about this subject in the same way that I said a few moments ago in another context I felt about a possible amendment that the hon. member for Halifax was going to move, namely, that we could not try to devise here and now a solution to this problem which would not create other problems that would also be very serious. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am going to ask the committee to agree that we direct the commission in this bill, not later than six months after the coming into force of the act, to embark upon a study of this question.
There are also a couple of small technical matters, one of which just corrects a misprint, but if the Minister of Fisheries would now move this amendment I would be very grateful.

What the hon. member for Calgary South and the hon. member for Medicine Hat have said is largely true. The only such pipe line project that has received much discussion is the one mentioned by the Shell Company, about which it made representations to the committee. I cannot conceive the Transport Commission would in the slightest degree be interested in dealing with matters relating to the construction of a pipe line, but the National Energy Board at present has no power under the law to regulate the tolls for commodities other than oil and gas. Thus there is a gap in the law.

EDUCATION-TORONTO-POSSIBLE CLOSING OF SCHOOLS FOR IMMIGRANT CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 13 I inquired of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration about a request presented to the government from the Toronto board of education for financial support from the federal government for language schools for immigrant children which
January 23, 1967
were threatened with closure for lack of funds.
One such school is known as the Main Street school in the east end of the city of Toronto. This one school alone provides accommodation for 132 pupils at a time. It gives special training to children of immigrants in the 13 to 17 year old bracket, so that they can be integrated into the regular school system. They stay at this special school as long as necessary so as to be able later to take full advantage of education in the ordinary system. The average stay of these pupils is six months, and in one year roughly 250 children of immigrants are taught English in order to fit them for ordinary schooling. The additional cost per pupil is roughly $538 per year, nearly double the ordinary cost of schooling. The total additional cost per year, therefore, is in the neighbourhood of $134,000.
I am raising this question, Mr. Speaker, as a matter of principle. It is my contention that the federal government, by reason of its responsibility in the field of immigration, has a duty to encourage and assist local authorities to shoulder this burden. In his reply the minister once again hid behind the tattered cloak of constitutional lack of responsibility, and as reported at page 11755 of Hansard said:
I think there is no federal responsibility in the field of language training in schools, even for immigrants.
I think the minister is wrong.
No one denies that the field of education generally belongs to the provinces. No one, at least not I, is suggesting that this be taken away. But it is the federal authority that seeks to encourage the admission of suitable immigrants to this country and that controls the flow of immigrants. It is the federal government that quite properly provides that immigrants are entitled and encouraged to bring their children and their families to this country. It is the federal government that recently published a white paper on Canada's immigration policy.
At page 139 of the white paper it is stated that people who come to Canada should receive the kind of services that they need to start productive employment in Canada. This, it says, means that they need language training. I suggest that obviously this does not apply to adults only; the entire white paper on immigration is geared to the idea that productive employment in the future will be based on literacy, education and adaptability.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
If children between the age of 13 and 17 years who come to Canada as immigrants with their parents are to be handicapped in their education by a deficiency in or lack of knowledge of the English language, this will affect their contribution to productive employment very likely throughout the whole of their working lives.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Chapter 6 of the white paper, which starts by extolling the virtues of co-operation, ends with these words:
Above all, satisfactory ways of improving language teaching facilities will be sought.
They will be sought by the government.
I suggest that one is entitled to wonder whether the Minister of Manpower and Immigration has read the white paper put out by his department. Discussing this matter, the Globe and Mail in an editorial on January 7 said this:
Manpower Minister Jean Marchand should be, if necessary, shamed into a similar position.
The editorial refers to a position of giving financial support to the maintenance of such schools.
Mr. Speaker, I hope even if my words are not sufficient to shame the minister, some members of his own party coming from constituencies where there are many immigrants and children of immigrants will shame the minister into changing his position. Certainly a government which trains adult immigrants and teaches them English, a government which accepts responsibility for training children of persons in the armed services, a government which I understand spends roughly $50 million a year on the education of Indian children, cannot shirk its responsibility for assisting immigrant children under the pretext of some imagined constitutional impotence. I hope the minister will consider this question carefully and announce a change of policy.

The hon. member has chosen to demonstrate that he is a lawyer, by scoffing at the law of the constitution as a tattered veil.
The minister is eager that all residents of Canada have the education or training they need to lead good lives in this country. This of

12152	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion course is obvious. I think even the hon. member for Greenwood would admit that a line must be drawn between those areas in which the government of Canada has a right to act and those in which the provinces have a right to act. The fact that a course of training or education will enable the person to enter into productive work in the economy sooner or later simply will not suffice as a definition of the federal area, because such a test-and this I think is what the hon. member proposes -would permit the federal government to swallow up all training and education.

I am also told that the department takes the view that language training for children, whether immigrants or persons born in Canada, is not its responsibility.

Consequently I think the chairman of the Toronto Board of Education ought to take this matter up with his provincial government. maintopic: AGRICULTURE-QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR PRICE DISCOUNT TO MILK CONSUMERS
AGRICULTURE-QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR PRICE DISCOUNT TO MILK CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 19 last I put the following question to the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene):
The minister is undoubtedly aware that the Quebec government has decided to increase the price of class I milk starting on February 1, 1967. Therefore, would he study the possibility of granting consumers a compensated discount of 10 cents per quart of milk to allow Canadian families to consume the milk they need for their health, especially that of their children?
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the Quebec government has just issued orders increasing the price of fluid milk for consumption purposes to $6 per hundredweight and, in certain areas, to as much as $6.65 per hundredweight, which will put the retail price up to 35 cents a quart.

DEBATES	January 23, 1967
It is not that producers are overpaid, far from it, because farmers have to satisfy milk production requirements that are becoming more and more exacting. They had to invest large amounts of money in order to improve their herds, and we all know that the cost of equipment, machinery and services required by farmers is constantly increasing, and we want farming to become a profitable undertaking.
But can the consumers bear the burden of this new increase in food cost? Each increase in the cost of living means a decrease in purchasing power, which is even now at a very low level. It is my fear that, as a result of this increase in the price of milk, consumption of the product will decrease considerably and children may be deprived of this commodity, so essential to their development. The October 1966 issue of Canadian Farm Economics contains the following statement at the bottom of page 3:
In the first semester of 1966, fluid milk consumption increased by about 1 per cent. Sales vary considerably from one area to another. A steady increase is expected in British Columbia, Alberta, New Brunswick and Ontario. In the other provinces, there has either been no change at all, or a very slight increase in sales. Consumption in Quebec has decreased, however.
The total sales of fluid milk in 1966 will probably not exceed the 5.2 billion pounds, I repeat, the 5.2 billion pounds sold last year.
Now, if the consumption of fluid milk decreases-no later than in 1962, 19.4 billion pounds of fluid milk were produced, whereas the expected production for 1967 will only be 18.2 billion pounds-producers will not be any better for it and everybody will lose by it.
Under a truly human and orderly economy, the purpose of production is consumption, and the latter must normally absorb the former. In order that milk production may reach the consumer and the latter may consume all he needs, the price must be within his means.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the spread between the price required by the milk producers-and the same could be said of many other products-and the price the consumer is in a position to pay is increasing more and more, and a reduction on fluid milk consumption will force the farmers either to reduce their production or to ship it to processing, which will reduce the returns. Let us avoid the grievous mistake of irritating the consumers and diverting them to less valuable products which will be accepted to the detriment of dairy farm sales and income.
January 23, 1967

To balance production and consumption prices and to enable the consumers to purchase milk at a reasonable price, the government should grant a compensated discount of 10 cents a quart on milk sold for fluid consumption, which would bring the price down to a reasonable level without reducing the producers' profits.
It will be remembered that, at the beginning of the 40's, a subsidy was granted on fluid milk. This had allowed an increase in the income of dairy farms and had promoted a greater consumption.
The minister will perhaps answer that this will cost many millions of dollars, but I would point out that consumers need milk, that it is produced that production could be increased. If the minister is short of credit, he needs only to turn to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and ask him to open the doors of the Bank of Canada. Thus, he will not have to levy new taxes. I will remind the minister that we give every year many millions of dollars to underdeveloped countries; while we are ourselves are becoming an underfed country. We can produce more and there is no reason why our people should be deprived of an essential commodity because of a lack of purchasing power.
When any area is prevented from producing according to the needs-

speechtext:

I should like to ask the minister whether he has been made aware of the unhappiness and concern that have arisen over the situation of an Indian agency superintendent acting as returning officer, having to cast a deciding ballot in the Brantford reserve elections. On the assumption that I wanted some detailed information about the situation on the Brantford reserve Your Honour suggested that I put the question on the order paper. However, since what I really had in mind were the broader questions which arose from the occurrence of this incident, I asked that the matter be put down for discussion at this time.

The fact that this expression of interest and concern took place is symptomatic of two things, first the growing desire of the Indian people for a broader and more complete measure of self-government within their bands, and second a growing awareness on the part of non-Indian people that this broader measure of self-government is something that the Indians of Canada should have.
When I read the report of this incident it seemed to me it was one of those rather unusual events which my own returning officer once told me was a nightmare for all returning officers, namely having to cast a deciding ballot in an election. In this case it must have been particularly embarrassing for the Indian agency superintendent, because obviously there was balanced opinion between members of the band as to who should be their chief councillor and he, as a non-Indian and public servant of Canada, was placed in the position of declaring in which direction he himself felt the choice should be made.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.>
It does seem to me that the Indian agency superintendent was acting in this capacity in line with the symbolic and traditional status
12154	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of Indians; that is, wards of the Queen. In this regard I think the situation is not all it might be.
I will agree that during a transitional period, directed toward increased self-government within Indian bands, some help and assistance in the techniques of elections and the exercise of what is considered by non-Indians to be the process of democracy, should be made available. However, I do believe that some steps should be taken to avoid the possible recurrence of this kind of situation.
It is my hope that the minister will consider that in the matter of band elections it would be desirable to select someone not engaged in the Indian affairs branch of his department as a returning officer, preferably someone chosen by the members of the band, and preferably an Indian-either a member of that band or of some other band.
It does seem to me that such a step would be a step toward making it clear that those of us here in parliament, and particularly those of us who hope that the functions of the Indian affairs branch will in the present and foreseeable future undergo a rather rapid transformation in its basic functions, have a desire that Indians should become self-governing. I am interested now in hearing a reply from the minister as to what steps he has in mind regarding the situation which has developed on this particular reserve.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-BRANTFORD, ONT.-DECIDING VOTE CAST BY RETURNING OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter raised by the hon. member for Commox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) relates to a vote which took place for the position of band chief of the Six Nations Reserve on December 17 last. As a result of that election Mr. Richard Isaac and Mr. Keith Martin were tied with 123 votes each.
I am of the opinion, as the hon. member indicated, that in such cases the lot of a returning officer, like that of a policeman, is not a happy one. That is no doubt why successive governments have been extremely careful in appointing returning officers for our elections, so that if a situation like this arose they would know enough to do the right thing.
The situation here was unfortunate, in that we had foreseen this difficulty as a result of a similar tie vote and had circularized all Indian bands in Canada with the suggestion that
DEBATES	January 23, 1967
we did not want our people involved. We asked them to see to it that an Indian be appointed as the returning officer.
The band met on this point on December 1. The result was that they insisted that our agency superintendent, Mr. Cassie, act as returning officer, which he did. We are now trying to break the tie by having a recount of ballots, and we have asked for an identification of the difficulties experienced in respect of those ballots that were spoiled.
In the meantime we have suggested to our superintendents that wherever possible an Indian should be appointed as a returning officer and, if necessary, the superintendent should act as deputy returning officer in order to give the required assistance. We have also asked the National Indian Advisory Board for its views of the suggestion that we enact a regulation to make this procedure mandatory; in other words make it mandatory that a member of the band be appointed as the returning officer.
In the case now under review, Mr. Keith Martin, the unsuccessful candidate for chief, has submitted an official appeal. This is currently under consideration, and as one preliminary step we have asked that the ballots be re-examined by the electoral officer who will provide a physical description of the spoiled ballots. As an adjunct of the re-examination, all the ballots will again be tabulated and recorded before appropriate witnesses.
In conclusion, I might mention that a similar situation arose in the Six Nations election in December, 1963. At that time Mr. Keith Martin, who is appealing the latest by-election, ran as a councillor in district No. 4. On that previous occasion Mr. Martin tied with another candidate for councillor and it was necessary for the electoral officer to cast a deciding vote to break the tie. In that instance the then superintendent, in his capacity as electoral officer, voted in favour of Mr. Martin.
I think our people would very much like to be rid of this responsibility, and we think we can bring this about by amending the regulations. In this regard we want the approval of the National Indian Advisory Board. I thank the hon. member for raising this matter.
